name: @examples/dev-harness
//dependencies: The harness is a workspace dependency because this example *is* its end-to-end case:
`vp dev` here runs the real plugin against a real `forguncy.config.ts`, which is what makes
it evidence rather than an illustration.
`@forguncy-react-workspace/runtime` is the façade the Cell's authored source imports by name.
It is a *source* dependency rather than a deployed module: the compiler flattens it into the
artifact like any other source file (#14), and the dev server resolves it as source through
this workspace link. Its being flattened per Cell is also what makes the façade's single
`@forguncy-react-workspace/core` is not a dependency: nothing in `src/` imports it, and the
config file's `defineForguncyConfig` is the only use — which arrives through the workspace
root's resolution. Nothing in the Cell's own module graph reaches `core`, which is the point
of the Cell's source importing only the façade.
`react` is deliberately NOT a dependency, for the rule `examples/host-antd/package.json`
records at length: `react` is decided `host`, the bridge intercepts the specifier before node
resolution, and installing it would be a silent escape hatch for a broken interception. Under
`vp dev` the harness supplies the substitution from its own pinned dependency instead, which
is the arrangement that keeps this example's `package.json` honest about what the page owns.
//scripts: There is no `dev` script, on purpose: `vp dev` — the bare built-in command, no flags and no
wrapper — is the local loop for this example, which is what #22's Developer workflow spells
out and what #23's first acceptance criterion says. The script this file used to carry
(`vp dev --configLoader runner`) is gone now that it is no longer needed; keeping a script
that resolves to the same thing would only be a place for the two to disagree.
Why the flag was needed, recorded here so the next project with workspace TypeScript packages
does not rediscover it (#67):
Vite's default config loader (`bundle`) externalizes every import in `vite.config.ts` that
resolves into node_modules, and this repository's workspace packages are *source*: they are
linked into node_modules but their `exports` point at `.ts` files. A bundled-then-node-loaded
config therefore died with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND: Cannot find module
.../packages/core/src/ownership`, because node ESM requires an extension on a relative import
and the config bundler deliberately did not rewrite one.
The fix that makes bare `vp dev` work is in the *packages*, not here: every relative import in
`packages/**` and `examples/**` now names its file with a `.ts`/`.tsx` extension (see the
`allowImportingTsExtensions` note in the root `tsconfig.json`). Node then resolves the config's
externalized workspace imports directly, so no `configLoader` override is needed and no wrapper
script is needed to supply one.
`runner` was the earlier workaround and is not used: it loads the config through Vite's own
module runner, which resolves the extensionless imports but is documented experimental. The
extension is the smaller dependency on behavior nobody promised.
Why the flag could not simply be set in `vite.config.ts`: Vite reads `configLoader` *before* it
reads the config file, so the setting always arrived too late. And `vp dev` is a built-in
command that a `package.json` script cannot override — `vp run dev` reaches the script instead —
which is why the old workaround had to change *how the command was invoked at all*. Both facts
are still true; they just no longer matter, because the resolution now works without them.
//devDependencies: `@forguncy-react-workspace/core` is a devDependency rather than a dependency because its only
use is `defineForguncyConfig` in the committed config, which Vite loads itself. The Cell's
module graph never reaches it — asserted in the example's own test, which checks that the
compiled artifact carries no copy of it.
